newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGB futures end lower, await benchmark shift.
newsitem.headline: JGB futures end lower, await benchmark shift.

text.p: The key June 10-year Japanese government bond futures contract ended lower on Tuesday on technical selling ahead of a shift forward in benchmark status from the June to the September, traders said.
"The only thing that was being sold was the June. The September was (relatively) firm, and there was some buying on dips of cash bonds," a brokerage house trader said.
Buying of cash bonds was by dealers who needed to cover short positions, the trader said.
Traders said investors took a wait-and-see stance ahead of the release of the Bank of Japan's "tankan" survey on June 25.
The June's weakness relative to the September was probably due to the rolling over of long positions ahead of a shift forward in benchmark status, the brokerage house trader said.
"Some players who had long positions in the June were selling June and buying September," the trader said.
The June may also have been hurt by firmness in Tokyo share prices, some traders said.
The June ended at 123.75, down from Monday's close of 124.00. Turnover was 35,102 contracts.
The September ended at 122.35, down slightly from Monday's close of 122.41. Turnover was 24,961 contracts.

Traders said they expected the September to take over the benchmark mantle on Wednesday. The September will become the new benchmark futures contract when its turnover over an entire trading day exceeds that of the June.
A trader for a city bank's securities unit said this was the first time that a shift in benchmark status to the September contract had failed to take place before the month of June.
"It is really taking a long time for the benchmark contract to change, especially when considering that the June's last trading date is on June 9," the brokerage house trader said.
Comments by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka late in the morning session, saying he shared the concerns of those dependent on interest income, had only a limited impact on JGBs, traders said.
"Dealers sold briefly afterwards, but they were forced to buy back when investors refrained from joining in the selling," a city bank trader said.
Mitsuzuka told a parliamentary committee on Tuesday: "I have told them (people dependent on interest rate income) to please hang on for a little while longer. We need to move towards stable growth."
Mitsuzuka's comments were offset by the Bank of Japan governor's view that the current low interest rate policy is helping Japan's economic recovery, the first trader said.

BOJ Governor Yasuo Matsushita told the same parliamentary committee: The low rate policy has increased corporate activity and is contributing towards the economy's self-sustaining recovery. We believe this is important."
The benchmark 182nd JGB yield stood at 2.560 percent as of 0700 GMT, up from the previous day's close of 2.545 percent.
In the Tokyo stock market, the key Nikkei 225 average ended at 20,563.16, up 111.31 points or 0.54 percent from Monday.
